newsitem.title: FRANCE: Suez Lyonnaise stock rises, investors await action.
newsitem.headline: Suez Lyonnaise stock rises, investors await action.

text.p: Shares in newly merged Suez Lyonnaise des Eaux have rewarded investors since their debut on the Paris bourse a month ago but unless the company acts soon to reinforce their confidence, the honeymoon could prove short-lived, analysts said.

They said the company's wide spread of holdings, grouped into an old-fashioned French corporate structure, offered a short-term source of cash from asset sales that would boost results and give the company some financial room for manoeuvre.

But the long term health of the sprawling multinational depends on a targeted programme of concentration -- probably through asset sales -- on its core businesses of energy, water and waste management.

Suez Lyonnaise, a behemoth with 200 billion francs in turnover formed by the merger on June 19 of Groupe Suez and Lyonnaise des Eaux, has holdings ranging from consumer credit to television channels, water utilities and waste management.

"I'm a bit reserved with regard to this new group, which looks a little too much like a conglomerate," said a Paris-based analyst. "Lyonnaise, which had restructured pretty well, is now a conglomerate again."

Granted it has a lot of potential, it can generate a lot of cash, but I find there is not too much to be enthusiastic about in the short term. We're going to get results bloated by exceptional events and capital gains."
The Paris stock market has shown much less hesitation about the merger since the new company began trading on June 30.
It has climbed 17 percent since then, outstripping the blue chip CAC-40 stock index which was 4.6 percent higher.
Several analysts are targetting 750 francs in the medium term for the share. It was trading at 691 francs on Friday, off its year high of 716 francs set on July 17.

Several dealers said much of the gain was driven by a simple logic of pushing the share price toward that of Compagnie Generale des Eaux, Suez Lyonnaise's main rival. Generale des Eaux was trading at 738 francs on Friday.

Analysts said the company would have to make hard decisions about what represented core, strategic assets, and added that the fate of its small communications businesses and huge financial holdings were key.

Early signs from the company hold out hope that its management, headed by former Suez chairman Gerard Mestrallet, understands how important concentration on core businesses is for the firm, they said.
On July 9, Suez-Lyonaise unit Societe Generale de Belgique sold 24 percent of its stake in Union Miniere, producing a capital gain of 12 billion Belgian francs.
"The sale of 24 percent of Union Miniere was a good first step and we are waiting for other strategic decisions," said the Paris-based analyst.
Analysts expressed confidence in Mestrallet, who stripped the ailing Groupe Suez of non-core assets to prepare it for the merger with Lyonnaise.
But he clearly has his work cut out.
"I wouldn't say that communications fits that well into this structure," said Susan Witt, analyst with Standard and Poor's.
Suez Lyonnaise communications units, with Lyonnaise Cable, television channel M6 and the TPS satellite television venture, account for only one percent of the company's turnover.
"It's very hard to say whether they can keep going as a small player. Unless they can get a leading position in a sizeable market somewhere, it's hard to see them making a lot of money out of it."
Witt and other analysts noted however that Suez Lyonnaise could decide to push hard into communications and was theoretically capable of making a success of it.
"They can invest in communications but we have to watch these investments closely to be sure they don't pay too much and that they are profitable," said an analyst.
Most analysts said the company would probably have to shed its huge financial holdings, too, but over a much longer period of time.
"The whole justification of the merger was an industrial utility company so it's a bit difficult to figure out why the financial subsidiaries are there," Witt said.
"They don't need to sell these businesses anytime soon; some of them are quite good businesses and they're not about to sell them just to follow a strategy," Witt said.
"But looking further out, in 10 years I'd be surprised if they still had them."
